meta_jurisdiction_context.legal_system_doctrine: Common Law (Federal State) - Alberta applies the common law tradition, modified by federal and provincial statutes under the federal-provincial division of powers

Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP)

ubo_and_aml_profiling.statutory_law_governance: Business Corporations Act (Alberta), RSA 2000, c B-9, ss. 21.1-21.4 (Register of Individuals with Significant Control and UBO disclosure duties); Corporate Registry Regulation (Alberta) (name clearance, registration, and fee rules); Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act, SC 2000, c 17 (federal AML/CFT statute administered by FINTRAC, including obligations of trust and company service providers); Criminal Code, RSC 1985, c C-46, ss. 462.3 et seq. (money laundering and proceeds-of-crime offences); Income Tax Act, RSC 1985, c 1 (5th Supp.) (beneficial ownership and reporting rules); Canada Business Corporations Act, RSC 1985, c C-44, ss. 21.1-21.4 (federal ISC register for comparison and federal filings if the parent is Canadian)
ubo_and_aml_profiling.ubo_disclosure_level: Government_Only_Access - the Alberta ULC must maintain an internal Register of Individuals with Significant Control which is not publicly searchable in the Alberta Corporate Registry; it must be produced on demand to the Registrar, FINTRAC, law enforcement, and tax authorities; a federal publicly accessible beneficial ownership registry for federal corporations is being phased in separately

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.document_name: Certificate of Good Standing / Certificate of Status of the sole corporate shareholder (foreign parent)
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: Competent corporate registry of the parent company's state of incorporation (e.g., Secretary of State or equivalent authority)
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: Hague Apostille - Canada acceded to the Apostille Convention on 12 May 2023 and it entered into force on 11 January 2024; consular legalization is required only if the origin state is not an Apostille Convention party

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.document_name: Certified copy of the certificate of incorporation and charter documents of the sole corporate shareholder
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: Competent corporate registry of the parent company's state of incorporation
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: Hague Apostille, or consular legalization for instruments originating outside Apostille Convention states

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.document_name: Certificate of Incumbency listing officers and directors of the sole corporate shareholder
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: Corporate secretary or authorized officer of the sole corporate shareholder
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: Notarization followed by Hague Apostille issued by the parent's state competent authority

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.document_name: Duly notarized board resolution of the sole corporate shareholder authorizing incorporation of the Alberta ULC, appointment of initial directors, and approval of the incorporation steps
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: Board of directors of the sole corporate shareholder, notarized
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: Hague Apostille for use in Alberta; consular legalization if executed outside an Apostille Convention state

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.issuing_entity: Notary public in the jurisdiction of residence of each individual
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: Hague Apostille for each notarial certificate; consular legalization for non-Apostille countries; Canadian-resident individuals may use Canadian notarization without apostille for registry filing

mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.document_name: Bank reference letter / confirmation of financial standing of the sole corporate shareholder
mandatory_notarization_and_apostille_bun.authentication_path: Notarization and Hague Apostille, or recognized foreign notarization protocol of the bank's home jurisdiction

ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: Mandatory screening of all directors, officers, individuals with significant control (25% or more), and authorized representatives against: (1) FINTRAC guidance and PCMLTFA verification and record-keeping rules applied by the law firm and corporate service provider as reporting entities; (2) Canadian sanctions regulations under the Special Economic Measures Act and the United Nations Act, administered by Global Affairs Canada and Public Safety Canada; (3) UN Security Council Consolidated List; (4) OFAC SDN, SSI, and Non-SDN lists, required by the target payment rails (Shopify Payments, PayPal, and Stripe); (5) UK HMT and EU consolidated sanctions lists; (6) domestic and foreign Politically Exposed Persons (PEP) screening per FINTRAC PEP guidance, including heads of international organizations; automatic enhanced due diligence (EDD) upon any positive match, adverse media, or nexus to a high-risk jurisdiction; findings documented in the pre-incorporation AML file and re-run before share issuance and director appointment.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: Alberta Corporate Registry (Service Alberta) - name clearance conducted through the NUANS (Newly Upgraded Automated Name Search) system using the official Alberta Corporate Registry portal or an authorized Alberta corporate service provider
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: Corporate names must be in English or French characters (or a combination), rendered in the Roman alphabet; foreign-script names must be transliterated into romanized form; the name must contain a distinctive element and one of the statutory legal elements for an unlimited liability corporation - 'Unlimited Liability Corporation', 'ULC', or the French equivalents; permitted punctuation is limited to periods, hyphens, apostrophes, ampersands, and similar standard marks; non-Roman characters are not accepted
prohibited_and_sensitive_tokens: Bank (requires federal/provincial financial institution regulator approval)
Trust or Trust Company (reserved for licensed trust entities)
Insurance or Assurance (reserved for licensed insurers)
Loan or Loan Corporation (requires financial regulator consent)
University, College, or Institute (requires ministry or educational authority consent)
Engineer or Engineering (requires APEGA professional body consent)
Architect (requires Alberta Association of Architects consent)
Lawyer, Barrister, or Solicitor (requires Law Society of Alberta consent)
Accountant, Auditor, or Chartered (requires CPA Alberta consent)
Royal, King, Queen, Government, or Crown (implies Crown connection; requires ministerial consent or waiver)
Alberta (use of the provincial name requires Government of Alberta consent where it implies government endorsement)
Cooperative or Credit Union (reserved for registered cooperatives and financial cooperatives)
Words that are obscene, scandalous, or imply insolvency, criminality, or prohibited activity (prohibited absolutely)
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: A NUANS-based name reservation is valid for 90 days and cannot be extended; upon rejection, the applicant may: (1) file a written reconsideration request with the Registrar of Corporations (Service Alberta) within 30 days of the rejection, attaching a new or renewed NUANS report and any required regulatory consents; (2) reapply with a revised distinctive element where the rejection is based on confusing similarity; or (3) apply to the Court of King's Bench of Alberta for judicial review of the Registrar's decision under the Business Corporations Act (Alberta) if reconsideration is denied; in parallel, a fresh name reservation request should be filed to prevent expiry of the proposed name during the appeal.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: Permissible for an e-commerce DTC brand with no physical retail footprint. The Business Corporations Act (Alberta) requires a registered office situated in Alberta with a physical street address (not a post office box) where process may be served, plus a separate records address. A licensed virtual office or corporate registered agent service satisfying these address requirements is accepted by the Alberta Corporate Registry and the Canada Revenue Agency for a Shopify-based business, provided the ULC maintains substantive corporate records and a registered agent able to accept service during business hours.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: Low - approximately 5-10% probability over a 12-month cycle for a low-risk, standard-tier e-commerce entity (ISIC 4791 / NAICS 454110). The Alberta Corporate Registry performs mostly documentary review tied to annual returns and address verification; CRA GST/HST and income tax audits are document-driven and typically conducted remotely; unannounced physical inspection of the registered office is unlikely unless the entity is flagged for fraud indicators, shell-company characteristics, undisclosed PEP ownership, or sanctions nexus, in which case the probability increases materially.

incorporation_legal_framework.governing_statute_and_sections: Business Corporations Act (Alberta), RSA 2000, c. B-9; article filing and certificate provisions in sections 12-16; registered office, director and officer provisions in sections 101-110; unlimited liability company provisions as applicable
incorporation_legal_framework.competent_registry_authority: Alberta Corporate Registry, Service Alberta / Registrar of Corporations
incorporation_legal_framework.statutory_filing_instrument: Articles of Incorporation and Initial Registered Office Information; issuance of Certificate of Incorporation by the Registrar
incorporation_legal_framework.minimum_paid_up_capital_rule: No statutory minimum paid-up capital is required; share consideration is payable in accordance with the articles or share subscription agreement. No escrow account or capital blocking rule applies to an Alberta ULC.
incorporation_legal_framework.pro_forma_first_board_resolution_en: RESOLVED, that the Articles of Incorporation filed with the Alberta Corporate Registry are adopted and confirmed, and each founding shareholder's subscription for the classes and numbers of shares set forth in the share subscription register is approved. RESOLVED FURTHER, that the registered office of the corporation is fixed at [full address], Alberta, and [registered agent name] is appointed as registered agent for service of process. RESOLVED FURTHER, that [names] are elected as the first directors, and [names] are appointed as Chief Executive Officer, Chief Financial Officer, and Corporate Secretary, each to serve in accordance with the bylaws and the Business Corporations Act (Alberta).

step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Alberta Corporate Registry CORES online portal / authorized NUANS search provider
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Submit a name reservation request through CORES using the proposed DTC brand name and at least two alternate names. Pay the NUANS search fee, obtain the name search report, and await the name reservation response before proceeding with incorporation.
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the name is refused, file a new reservation with amended names or request a formal review by the Registrar demonstrating that the proposed name is distinguishable from existing conflicting marks.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Filing of Articles of Incorporation and Registered Office Information
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Registrar of Corporations, Alberta Corporate Registry (CORES or authorized service provider)
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Complete the prescribed incorporation form on CORES, including the exact corporate name, share structure, first directors, and registered office address in Alberta. Attach the name reservation confirmation and consent to act as director forms. Pay the statutory filing fee. Upon approval, the Registrar issues the Certificate of Incorporation.
required_dossiers: Consent to Act as Director from each director
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If the application is queried, file a corrected amended statement within 30 days through CORES. If refusal is maintained, the applicant may pursue a formal appeal or re-file after curing the stated deficiency.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Adoption of Bylaws, Appointment of Officers and Share Issuance
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Hold the first board meeting or execute a written resolution. Adopt the corporation's bylaws, approve the first share subscription, issue share certificates, elect officers, establish the fiscal year end, and approve the corporate seal and bank account resolution for the DTC brand.
required_dossiers: Notice of first board meeting or written consent resolution
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: Rectify governance defects by supplemental director resolution. If share issuance is invalidated, issue corrective share certificates or apply for a court validation order under the Business Corporations Act (Alberta).

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Establishment of Registered Office Records and Statutory Registers
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Prepare the corporate minute book and maintain all statutory registers at the registered office, including registers of directors, officers, shareholders, and transfers. Confirm the registered office address and ensure records are available for inspection in accordance with the Business Corporations Act (Alberta).
required_dossiers: Shareholder register and share transfer register
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If statutory records are deficient, immediately file corrected registers and resolutions. If the corporation is administratively dissolved for record-keeping default, apply for reinstatement under the applicable Alberta reinstatement process.

step_by_step_formation_sop.step_name: Confirmation of Business Licensing and Non-Industrial Status
step_by_step_formation_sop.competent_authority: Municipal business licensing office (where applicable) and Alberta Environment and Protected Areas
step_by_step_formation_sop.detailed_action_protocol: Verify that no statutory industrial or manufacturing license is required for ISIC 4791 (online DTC retail). If the brand operates from commercial office or warehouse premises, obtain the applicable municipal business licence and complete fire safety and basic workplace inspections. For pure digital operations, document the exemption.
required_dossiers: Business premise lease or utility statement
Municipal business licence application (if premises exist)
Fire safety inspection clearance (if premises exist)
step_by_step_formation_sop.adverse_action_remedies: If a municipal licence or inspection is refused, cure zoning, building, or fire-code deficiencies and reapply, or lodge an appeal under the applicable municipal bylaw. No provincial industrial environmental review is triggered for a pure e-commerce activity.

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.competent_industrial_authority: Not applicable — no Alberta industrial licensing board exercises jurisdiction over internet retail operations.
industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.operating_license_title: No manufacturing or operating permit is required; retail sale via internet (DTC brand webstore) is not a statutorily licensed activity in Alberta.

environmental_impact_assessment_eia.classification_tier: Exempt — the activity does not require a mandatory environmental impact assessment under the Environmental Protection and Enhancement Act, RSA 2000, c. E-12.
environmental_impact_assessment_eia.discharge_and_emissions_standards: Not applicable to pure digital retail. If future warehousing or fulfillment operations are established, comply with the Waste Control Regulation (Alta. Reg. 192/1996) and the applicable air quality emission limits under the Alberta Air Quality Regulation (Alta. Reg. 328/2019).

industry_physical_and_environmental_lice.civil_defense_and_occupational_clearance: Not applicable for a home-office or virtual-webstore operation. If a commercial office, warehouse, or fulfillment centre is used, secure fire safety certification under the Safety Codes Act and comply with the OHS Code (Alta. Reg. 87/2009) for workplace health and structural load requirements.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) / Agence du revenu du Canada — national tax authority for federal income tax and GST/HST. Primary portal: CRA My Business Account (https://www.canada.ca/en/revenue-agency/services/e-services/digital-services-individuals/business-account.html) and Business Registration Online (BRO). Alberta corporate income tax is administered by CRA on behalf of the Province of Alberta Treasury Board and Finance under a federal-provincial Tax Collection Agreement. The statutory identifier is the 9-digit CRA Business Number (BN) plus program account suffixes (e.g., RT0001 for GST/HST; RC0001 for corporate income tax).
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: (1) Incorporate the Alberta Unlimited Liability Corporation (ULC) under the Alberta Business Corporations Act; the provincial corporate registry transmits incorporation data electronically to CRA, which auto-establishes the federal BN and corporate income tax program account. (2) Register the ULC for GST/HST through CRA Business Registration Online or by filing Form RC1 (and, for non-residents, Form GST355 'GST/HST Registration for Non-Residents'); CRA then issues the BN with an RT program account. (3) A non-resident corporation carrying on business in Canada through an establishment, warehouse, employee, or agent soliciting orders is deemed to carry on business in Canada (Excise Tax Act subsection 174(1)) and must register once gross worldwide taxable supplies exceed CAD 30,000 over four consecutive calendar quarters. (4) Exporters must also create a Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) exporter account through the CBSA Assessment and Revenue Management (CARM) portal and obtain a linked exporter identifier for filing B13A export declarations. (5) The ULC must open a Canadian-dollar bank account, display the BN on all invoices and customs documents, and maintain non-resident director/ownership records for CRA beneficial-ownership verification.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.default_entity_tax_classification: Pass_Through_Eligible — the Alberta ULC is a taxable Canadian corporation for domestic Income Tax Act purposes (entity-level taxation on worldwide income), but it is eligible for fiscally transparent/pass-through treatment under statutory elections and treaty rules. It qualifies for the Excise Tax Act subsection 256.1(4) election to be treated as a partnership for GST/HST purposes, and, where all members are residents of treaty countries, it may be treated as a flow-through entity for foreign tax purposes, giving rise to hybrid entity characteristics that are constrained by Canadian hybrid mismatch rules. It is not a Tax-Exempt Zone entity and has no territorial exemption; Canada taxes resident corporations on worldwide net income.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: (1) ETA subsection 256.1(4) check-the-box-style election: eligible entity election filed with CRA (Form GST26 series) to deem the ULC a partnership for GST/HST purposes, allowing members to be treated as partners; conditions include all members being individuals, or corporations resident in Canada, or residents of a country with which Canada has a tax treaty. (2) Income Tax Act subsections 18.2 and 18.4 hybrid mismatch defensive rules: deny interest deductibility where a deductible payment is made through a hybrid entity structure that produces a deduction without corresponding inclusion, including ULCs treated as disregarded entities in the United States. (3) Income Tax Act subsection 128.1(1) deemed disposition election upon change of residence status of the corporation. (4) Subsection 256.1(5) revocation election. (5) US federal Form 8832 check-the-box classification of the Canadian ULC may create a disregarded entity for US members; Canadian rules apply the MLI principal purpose test and treaty limitation-of-benefits provisions to counteract such mismatches.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: GST/HST — federal Goods and Services Tax / Harmonized Sales Tax value-added tax administered under the Excise Tax Act; Alberta applies only the 5% federal GST with no provincial sales tax or HST provincial component.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: CAD 30,000 — small-supplier threshold under ETA subsection 148(1): registration is mandatory once total worldwide taxable supplies (excluding zero-rated supplies) in the current quarter and preceding four calendar quarters exceed CAD 30,000; voluntary registration is available below the threshold. Non-resident suppliers of digital goods/services to Canadian consumers are subject to the simplified GST/HST registration regime without a Canadian permanent establishment, but generally retain the small-supplier exception only in narrow, Fact-limited cases.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: Canada does not impose a real-time fiscal clearance, continuous transaction control (CTC), or digital stamping mandate. No statutory API clearance or fiscal e-invoicing authorization is required at federal or Alberta level; however, GST/HST registered suppliers must issue tax invoices with prescribed content (ETA section 223) and retain records for six years. E-invoicing (EDI/PEPPOL or Shopify-generated invoices) is accepted, and returns must be filed electronically once thresholds are met. Effective July 2022, non-resident digital platform operators are deemed suppliers of GST/HST on marketplace sales made through their platforms; they must register, collect and remit tax, and provide prescribed seller data to CRA. A DTC brand selling through Shopify must verify whether the ULC or the Shopify platform operator holds the registration obligation depending on fulfillment location and seller-residency status.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: Goods: zero-rated under Schedule VI, Part V, section 12 of the Excise Tax Act where the supplier exports the goods in compliance with the Customs Act, delivers them to a common carrier for export, or transfers possession to a purchaser who immediately exports them. Services and intangible property: zero-rated under Schedule VI, section 23 (intangible personal property) and section 34 (services) when supplied to a non-resident who is not registered for GST/HST and the supply is not for consumption or use in Canada, excluding services related to real estate or tangible personal property situated in Canada. For the DTC brand: shipments of physical goods from Alberta/Canada to foreign ship-to addresses, downloads or cloud deliveries of digital products to non-resident customers, and subscription services rendered to non-residents all qualify, subject to proof of export, foreign destination, and settlement of foreign currency proceeds into the Canadian bank account of the ULC.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: Customs Export Declaration (CBSA B13A Export Declaration / CADEX electronic declaration where value exceeds CAD 2,000 or goods are regulated, with confirmation number and port of exit)
Bill of Lading or Air Waybill naming the ULC as exporter and showing the foreign port of discharge or destination
Inward Remittance Certificate — SWIFT MT103, PayPal/Stripe settlement statements, or bank credit advice evidencing receipt of export proceeds in the ULC's Canadian bank account in foreign currency
Commercial invoice and Shopify order report showing the foreign ship-to address, product description, quantity, and declared value
Carrier tracking and proof-of-delivery records (terminal receipt, port loading document, or courier 'delivered abroad' scan) establishing physical departure from Canada
Customs broker confirmation and the exporter's books and records retained for at least six years as required by the Excise Tax Act and the Income Tax Act record-retention rules
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: If export proof is missing or defective, CRA denies the zero-rating, reassesses the supply as taxable, and claws back uncollected GST/HST at 5% on the gross selling price, plus compound daily interest under ETA section 280.1. The normal reassessment limitation period is four years (ETA section 296); the period is unlimited in cases of misrepresentation, fraud, or wilful default. Penalties include: failure-to-file penalty of 5% plus 1% per month (ETA section 280); gross-negligence penalty of the greater of CAD 250 and 25% of the tax amount (ETA section 285); false-statement penalties and criminal tax evasion sanctions under ETA section 327 and Income Tax Act section 239, with fines up to 200% of the tax evaded and possible imprisonment. CRA's Exports Verification Unit and CBSA audits may deny related input tax credits, invoke the General Anti-Avoidance Rule, and reopen more than four prior years where documents are falsified; the Voluntary Disclosures Program may reduce penalties only if a qualifying disclosure is filed before the exporter is contacted by CRA.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Bank of Canada (BoC) together with the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions (OSFI) for prudential regulation, and the Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre of Canada (FINTRAC) for anti-money laundering/anti-terrorist financing compliance; no separate foreign-exchange control authority exists because Canada maintains a liberalized capital account.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: The Canadian dollar (CAD) is a fully convertible currency with no exchange controls or surrender obligations on current account transactions, trade settlements, dividend remittances, or capital account flows. Profit repatriation by a non-resident-owned Alberta ULC is generally unrestricted once statutory tax withholdings and arm’s-length transfer pricing documentation are satisfied; dividends, management fees, interest, and royalties are subject to Canadian withholding tax under the Canada-foreign treaty or Part XIII rates as applicable. There are no restrictions on maintaining foreign-currency bank accounts outside Canada; however, foreign-source capital inflows above CAD 10,000 are reportable to FINTRAC if in cash or virtual currency, and cross-border transfers may be subject to Canadian tax reporting (T1135 foreign income verification if applicable). Sanctions and anti-money-laundering measures (United Nations Act, Special Economic Measures Act, Freezing Assets of Corrupt Foreign Officials Act) can block transfers involving sanctioned jurisdictions or persons, so compliance screening is mandatory.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: Canada imposes no export-proceeds surrender requirements and no mandatory conversion of export receipts into CAD. Exporters may retain foreign currency in foreign or domestic bank accounts; however, the Canada Border Services Agency and Statistics Canada require accurate customs export declarations and trade-data reporting for goods movements, and FINTRAC requires transaction reporting for cross-border currency/electronic funds transfers exceeding CAD 10,000. For digital services sold via a Shopify DTC store, export proceeds are not deemed exports of physical goods for customs surrender purposes; the ULC must simply record revenue in CAD or functional currency under IFRS/ASPE and comply with the Income Tax Act’s section 12(1)(b) accrual rules where applicable.

tier1_domestic_commercial_banks.account_class: Canadian Dollar Operating and USD Non-Resident Foreign Currency Account
Operating Account with Treasury Management / Cross-Border Cash Management
Corporate Operating Account and Trade Finance Facilities
Operating Account and Foreign-Exchange/Wire Clearing Capabilities
Operating Account with Business Credit Card and Payment Rail Integration

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Medium. Offshore digital EMI/neo-bank providers (e.g., Wise, Interpago, Airwallex) may serve as payment-collection or foreign-currency settlement layer, but they are not licensed to take domestic Canadian deposits. To hold CAD deposits or operate as a payment service provider in Canada, a foreign EMI must be registered as a money services business (MSB) with FINTRAC and, depending on activities, may need to comply with the Retail Payment Activities Act (RPAA) administered by the Bank of Canada. Using a foreign EMI as the sole bank is not viable for ULC treasury needs; a tier-1 Canadian bank is required for CAD clearing, credit facilities, and regulatory confidence. Fintech rails are practical for Shopify Payments/PayPal/Stripe sub-merchant settlements but must route final treasury funds to the Canadian operating account.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: For a newly incorporated Alberta ULC with non-resident directors, most tier-1 banks mandate physical attendance by at least one director/signatory or a mandated executive for the initial KYC interview; branch-level ID verification is generally required for the first corporate account. Exception: fully remote video onboarding may be accepted when (a) the bank supports electronic identity verification, (b) all directors and beneficial owners hold current Canadian-issued photo ID or passports verifiable via certified/notarized foreign documents, (c) corporate registry extracts are apostilled or notarized, and (d) the expected transaction volume/risk profile is low. The ULC should prepare notarized powers of attorney and Alberta corporate resolution authorizing remote opening if signatories cannot travel.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Unlimited liability corporation / no minimum capital requirement
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Certificate of Incorporation, good standing certificate from Alberta Corporate Registry, notice of articles / by-laws showing directors, registered office, and authorized share structure; explanation of the commercial reason for ULC (cross-border tax consolidation/flow-through) and a signed written resolution acknowledging unlimited liability.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Non-resident beneficial ownership and foreign parent company
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Ultimate beneficial ownership (UBO) chart to natural persons, passport copies, proof of residential address, certificates of good standing for all corporate UBOs, source-of-funds evidence (audited financials, bank statements, tax filings), and any applicable Canada-U.S./foreign treaty certificate of residence (Form NR301) to support tax classification.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: High-volume DTC e-commerce flows through third-party payment processors (Shopify, PayPal, Stripe)
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Executed merchant agreements, platform payout schedules, chargeback and refund policies, revenue reporting extract from Shopify, and explanation of settlement cycle; evidence that sub-merchant funds do not cause third-party funds to flow through the ULC bank account in a way that would require licensing under PCMLTFA.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Cross-border wire activity and sanctions-screening risk
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Sanctions compliance policy, screening procedures against Canada’s consolidated Canadian Autonomous Sanctions List and OFAC/UN lists, counterparty due-diligence questionnaire, denied-party screening results, and prohibition on transactions with Russia, Belarus, Iran, North Korea, Syria, and Crimea/Donbas as applicable.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Source-of-funds opacity on capital injections from shareholder loans/equity
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Loan agreements, board resolutions, promissory notes, evidence of intercompany bookkeeping, recent audited financial statements of the funding parent, and confirmation that funding is not derived from proceeds of crime or tax evasion, supported by an accounting firm’s source-of-wealth letter.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: All capital injections into the Alberta ULC must be executed through formal intercompany loan or equity agreements, with proceeds transmitted via recognized wire networks only. In CAD: use SWIFT MT103 (with UETR) to the receiving bank’s CAD clearing account through Canada’s Large Value Transfer System (LVTS), or a domestic bill/EFT via Payments Canada if the sending party is in Canada. In USD: use SWIFT MT103 via correspondent U.S. banks clearing through Fedwire/CHIPS to the ULC’s USD account. The purpose-code line (Field 70/72 or bank-specific reason code) must specify “equity injection / direct investment” or “intercompany loan disbursement” and identify the ULC’s corporate registry number. Documentary evidence—board resolution, signed loan agreement/equity subscription, source-of-funds trail, and Alberta corporate registry confirmation—must be held by the bank’s compliance department. Investment Canada Act review is not required for the initial incorporation or internal reorganization of a new Canadian subsidiary, but acquisitions of an existing Canadian business by a non-Canadian parent must be assessed against the economic thresholds and National Security Review requirements.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: Outbound payments for supplier goods/services, software licensing, marketing expenses, and customs duties should be cleared using: (1) SWIFT MT103 wires with UETR and precise remittance information for large foreign payments via LVTS/correspondent banking; (2) commercial letters of credit (irrevocable, confirmed by a Canadian bank) or documentary collections where contracted terms require shipping documents against payment; (3) Payments Canada Automated Clearing Settlement System (ACSS) / Real-Time Rail (once fully operational) for domestic CAD supplier payments; (4) Shopify Payments/PayPal/Stripe settlement withdrawals to the operating account as the primary collection rail; and (5) cross-currency payment hubs via the ULC’s bank multi-currency account. All outgoing wire instructions must include invoice numbers, purchase order references, and sanctions-screening results, and must be approved under a dual-signatory authority matrix.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: CAD/USD spot and forward exchange contracts (delivery or delivery optional) with a licensed Canadian Schedule I bank or registered derivatives dealer
Cross-currency swaps (USD-CAD, EUR-CAD, GBP-CAD) under ISDA 2002 Master Agreement with credit support annex, subject to risk-management board approval

Non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) for hedges involving emerging-market currencies (e.g., CNH, INR, BRL) where CAD settlement is required, executed through bank treasury desks with established ISDA documentation
Plain vanilla foreign-exchange options (call/put on USD, EUR, GBP against CAD) designed to hedge forecast Shopify revenue receipts
Intercompany netting and matching programs through bank treasury portals to reduce FX exposures without entering into derivative contracts

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Alberta Annual Return (Corporate Annual Declaration under the Business Corporations Act, Alberta)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Alberta Corporate Registry - Service Alberta / RegistryXpress
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 60 days following each anniversary of incorporation; annual recurring filing on the corporation's anniversary date
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late filing penalty of CAD 50 plus CAD 50 for each additional uncompleted year; non-compliance for two consecutive years exposes the ULC to administrative strike-off and dissolution proceedings by the Registrar of Companies.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual General Meeting or Annual Unanimous Written Resolution in Lieu of Meeting
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Corporate Minute Book maintained at the Alberta registered office (no government filing required)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: First AGM within 18 months of incorporation; thereafter AGM no later than 15 months after the preceding AGM and in all cases within 6 months after fiscal year-end; a written resolution may substitute only with unanimous shareholder consent
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: No registry monetary penalty, but statutory default under the Alberta Business Corporations Act renders directors subject to court compliance orders and shareholders may apply for remedy, including oppression relief.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: T2 Corporation Income Tax Return (Federal and Alberta corporate income tax, filed jointly under the CRA-Alberta Tax Collection Agreement)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Return due within 6 months after fiscal year-end (e.g., June 30 following a December 31 year-end); final income tax balance remittance due within 2 months after year-end for non-CCPC corporations and within 3 months for eligible CCPCs claiming the small business deduction
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late-filing penalty of 5% of unpaid tax plus 1% per complete month (maximum 12 months), prescribed daily compound interest, gross negligence penalties on understatements, denial of loss carry-backs and director liability for unremitted amounts.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: GST/HST Return (Periodic or Annual Filing Election for Qualifying Small Suppliers)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Annual filers must file and remit within 3 months after fiscal year-end; monthly or quarterly filers must file within 1 month following the applicable reporting period
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late remittance penalty equal to 1% of the late amount plus 0.25% for each complete month up to 10 months, compounded daily prescribed CRA interest, and revocation of annual filing privileges for habitual non-compliance.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Notice of Change of Directors or Registered Office Address (Event-Driven Recurring Maintenance Filing)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Alberta Corporate Registry - Service Alberta / RegistryXpress
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Within 30 days after any change in directors or in the registered office or mailing address occurring during the compliance year
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Registry may assess late filing penalties per delinquent change instrument; outdated director/address data undermines valid service of process, financing transactions, good-standing certificates, and repeated default can precipitate administrative dissolution.

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual Appointment of Auditor or Unanimous Shareholder Waiver of Audit (ABCA ss. 160-161)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Corporate Minute Book and financial records held at the Alberta registered office (no government filing)
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Annually at the AGM or concurrently with fiscal year-end financial statement approval; the waiver must be unanimously consented to by all voting shareholders before the fiscal year financial statements are finalized
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Absence of a valid unanimous waiver automatically triggers the mandatory audit requirement; directors who fail to appoint an auditor are in statutory default and may be compelled by shareholder application or court compliance order.

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: No revenue or asset threshold applies under the Alberta Business Corporations Act; a mandatory independent audit arises when (i) the ULC is a distributing corporation, (ii) shareholders fail to execute the annual unanimous audit waiver, or (iii) the Registrar orders an audit. For income tax purposes, internally prepared unaudited financial statements are acceptable to the CRA, provided complete underlying books and records exist.
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: CPA Canada Handbook: IFRS is mandatory for publicly accountable enterprises; private ULCs may elect IFRS or Canadian ASPE (Accounting Standards for Private Enterprises, Handbook Part II). Financial statements are normally presented in CAD in conformity with the selected framework.

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: Alberta maintains an internal Register of Individuals with Significant Control (ISC) under the Alberta Business Corporations Act. There is no separate annual ISC filing to the provincial registry; the register must be updated on a rolling basis, reconciled at each fiscal year-end, and produced on lawful demand to the Registrar, police, and the Canada Revenue Agency. Before executing the annual return, management must reconfirm each shareholder's full legal name, residential address, and tax residence to keep the ISC register and annual return materially accurate.
mandatory_on_site_statutory_registers: Register of Directors (name, residential address, and dates of election and cessation)
Register of Individuals with Significant Control (ISC)
Minute Book (AGM minutes and unanimous resolutions)

recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.registered_office_or_agent_market_range_: USD 220-450 per year (CAD 300-600 typical Alberta registered office and registered agent market range)
recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.statutory_audit_estimated_fee_usd: USD 1,800-4,200 per year (CAD 2,500-5,700 typical for a low-volume DTC e-commerce ULC; avoidable while the annual unanimous audit waiver remains in force)

corporate_income_tax_regime.statutory_headline_rate: 23% federal rate plus 8% Alberta provincial rate for a combined 31% general corporate income tax rate; Alberta's 2% provincial rate applies to income eligible for the small business deduction, resulting in a 25% combined rate on the first CAD 500,000 of active business income for a Canadian-controlled private corporation (CCPC). A ULC is not a CCPC unless it meets the CCPC definition under subsection 125(7) of the Income Tax Act (Canada) (ITA), so the general rate of 31% is the default for most ULCs.
corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: For a ULC resident in Canada, no federal or Alberta provincial statutory tax holiday is generally available for retail e-commerce activities. A ULC may deduct ordinary and necessary business expenses under section 9 of the ITA and the matching Alberta Income Tax Act (AITA). Eligible capital cost allowance (CCA) rates apply under Schedule II of the Income Tax Regulations; Class 50 computer hardware at 55% declining balance, Class 12 computer software at 100%, and Class 14.1 eligible capital property at 5% declining balance. The federal manufacturing and processing profits deduction under section 125.1 of the ITA and the Atlantic investment tax credit under section 127 of the ITA are not applicable to a Shopify e-commerce retailer. A ULC is not entitled to the federal small business deduction unless it qualifies as a Canadian-controlled private corporation, which requires, among other conditions, that the corporation be resident in Canada, not controlled by non-residents, and not controlled by one or more public corporations. An Alberta ULC with non-resident owners is generally taxable as a corporation, not as a flow-through entity, for Canadian income tax purposes; the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) confirmed in Interpretation Document 2015-0634701C17 that a BC ULC is treated as a corporation for the purposes of the ITA unless subsection 125.7(5) applies. The Alberta ULC statute, the Business Corporations Act (Alberta), RSA 2000, c B-9 (ABCA), specifically states that a ULC is a corporation and holds itself out as a corporation. No Alberta provincial tax credit relevant to DTC retail.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: Federal: T2 Corporation Income Tax Return filed with the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) via CRA My Business Account, Represent a Client, or CRA-approved tax preparation software using electronic filing (EFILE) or internet filing (NETFILE). Alberta: Schedule K (Alberta Corporate Income Tax Return) is a component of the federal T2 return and is filed with the CRA as the single administration portal for federal and Alberta corporate taxes. T2 is an annual return. Alberta corporate income tax is administered by the CRA under a tax collection agreement; the Alberta Ministry of Treasury Board and Finance receives the provincial allocation through the T2 filing. The T2 return must be completed in Canadian dollars. Filing frequency: Annual, regardless of whether the corporation had taxable income or was dormant.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: The T2 return must be filed within six months after the end of the corporation's taxation year. For a December 31 year-end, the statutory filing deadline is June 30 of the following calendar year. A ULC with non-resident directors or shareholders must still file within six months of its fiscal year-end; no extension is available for non-residents except for a standard six-month filing deadline. If the corporation is non-resident and carries on business in Canada through a permanent establishment, the same six-month rule applies to the portion of income taxable in Canada. Balance due payment deadline: the full tax balance is due no later than the last day of the second month following the taxation year-end (i.e., February 28 for a December 31 year-end), and monthly instalments may be required if the corporation's federal/provincial tax payable exceeds CAD 3,000 in the current or prior year. Interest on late or deficient instalments compounds daily at the prescribed CRA rate (currently approximately 9% for 2025, set quarterly).

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: T2 – Page 1, Line 10: Identification and business address
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Corporate legal name, corporation number, business number (BN), taxation year start and end dates, jurisdiction of incorporation (Alberta), registered office address, and the principal business activity using the North American Industry Classification System (NAICS) code 454110 for electronic shopping and mail-order houses.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: A non-resident-owned ULC must indicate its residency status for tax purposes, provide the jurisdiction of incorporation as Alberta, and list the non-resident owners' names and addresses in the applicable schedule if the corporation is a specified foreign investment entity or if the non-resident ownership triggers the requirements of section 116 of the ITA or subsection 212(13.1) of the ITA. Use code 99 or the appropriate residency code to identify the corporation as a non-resident-owned corporation if applicable. A dormant ULC must still complete the identification schedule and check the 'dormant' box on the T2 return.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Gross revenue from the DTC e-commerce store, including Shopify Payments, PayPal, Stripe settlement amounts, shipping charged to customers, net of refunds, discounts, rebates, and sales taxes (GST/HST if the corporation is a registrant). Include all sales through the Shopify storefront, including sales to Canadian and export customers; export sales are Part of revenue and must be reported in Canadian dollars translated from foreign currencies using the CRA published annual or quarterly average exchange rates or the Bank of Canada noon exchange rates.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: For a ULC that is resident in Canada, worldwide revenue is taxable; therefore, include all foreign-source revenue. For a non-resident ULC with Canadian business income, include only revenue attributable to the Canadian permanent establishment. Currency translation: use the CRA exchange rate for the date of the transaction or an acceptable average annual rate.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: T2 – Page 2, Lines 30–80: Deductions and net income
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: COGS, advertising (Shopify Ads, Meta, Google), payment processing fees, Shopify subscription, hosting, domain, fulfillment and warehousing, freight, shipping supplies, chargebacks, depreciation/CCA, wages and contractors, professional fees, insurance, rent, and other expenses. Deductions must be reasonable and incurred for the purpose of earning income; promoter fees and shareholder personal expenses are not deductible.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Expenses must be allocated to the Canadian permanent establishment on a reasonable basis. Non-resident corporations cannot deduct head-office expenditures charged to the Canadian branch unless they are incurred for the purpose of earning Canadian income and are reasonable in amount; the ITA imposes a limit under subsection 161.5(1) for the allowance of branch accounting allocations. Transfer pricing rules under section 247 of the ITA require arm's length terms for intercompany charges on marketing, management, and administrative services. A ULC must not deduct payments made to non-arm's length non-residents unless contemporaneous documentation supports the amounts and the payments are subject to Canadian withholding tax where applicable.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: T2 – Page 3, Lines 100–126: Taxable income and Part I tax
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Compute taxable income by deducting loss carryovers, non-taxable dividends received (under section 112 of the ITA if from a taxable Canadian corporation), capital gains reserve, and any prior-year losses. Compute federal Part I tax at the 23% general rate on taxable income, then deduct federal foreign tax credits, investment tax credits, and the general rate reduction. Enter Alberta corporate income tax on Schedule K or T2CO-AB.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: A non-resident corporation with a permanent establishment in Canada computes taxable income only on Canadian-source business income. A ULC that is a non-resident-owned investment corporation (NRO) may be subject to special Part I rules and Part XIII withholding tax on distributions. If the ULC is a resident of Canada but owned by US persons, check the Application of the Canada–US Tax Convention for any exemption or reduction in Part XIII withholding tax on interest or royalties.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: T2 – Page 3, Line 350: Investment tax credits and other credits
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Claim federal and Alberta investment tax credits, foreign tax credits, and political contribution tax credits if applicable. A DTC e-commerce retailer generally has no significant investment tax credits except for the digitalization and scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) credit if the corporation performs qualified technology development in Canada.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Non-resident corporations may claim foreign tax credits only to the extent the foreign taxes are paid on Canadian-source income recognized under the relevant tax treaty. SR&ED is available only to persons carrying on business in Canada through a permanent establishment; a non-resident ULC may claim if the permanent establishment performs the eligible work.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: Schedule 1 / T2SCH1: Net income (loss) before adjustments
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Detailed reconciliation of accounting net income to tax net income, including adjustments for CCA, non-deductible meals and entertainment (50%), non-deductible fines and penalties, and other timing and permanent differences.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: For a non-resident ULC, use the branch accounting rules in ITA sections 1, 2, and 4, and the permanent establishment regulations in ITA subsections 402(1)–(7), to allocate income to Canada. The Schedule 1 reconciliation must be prepared in Canadian dollars and must exclude income that is not attributable to the Canadian PE.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Disclosure of all shareholders, their jurisdiction of residence, percentages of voting and equity ownership, and any exchange-listed status. For a ULC, this schedule captures the full statutory unlimited liability structure; the CRA requires the ultimate beneficial owner for each shareholder, including non-residents.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: For a ULC with non-resident shareholders, provide each shareholder's country of residence for tax treaty purposes, their social insurance number or foreign tax identification number, and the Canadian agent for service if applicable. Failure to disclose non-resident ownership can trigger penalties under subsection 162(7) and can disqualify a ULC from the small business deduction if the non-resident control threshold is crossed.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: Schedule 31 / T2SCH31: Foreign income/expense and foreign tax credits
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Attribution of business income earned in foreign jurisdictions, foreign taxes paid, and calculation of the federal foreign tax credit under sections 126 and 127 of the ITA. For an online retailer, revenues from US and non-Canadian customers are sourced according to the 'place where the sale occurs' rule under section 253B of the ITA as modified by the Canada-US treaty and other DTAs.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: For a Canadian-resident ULC, include all foreign business income on Schedule 31 to claim foreign tax credits. For a non-resident ULC with a Canadian PE, the Schedule 31 should reflect only taxes paid to foreign jurisdictions on income that is also included in the Canadian taxable income of the PE, subject to the treaty tie-breaker and permanent establishment rules under each DTA.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: Schedule K (Alberta): T2CO-AB Alberta corporate income tax
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Compute Alberta taxable income, which generally begins with federal taxable income and applies Alberta-specific adjustments. Alberta uses a single 8% general corporate rate; the provincial rate applied to income eligible for the Alberta small business deduction is 2% for an eligible CCPC. Alberta does not impose capital tax, franchise tax, or payroll tax on the ULC's net income.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: A non-resident ULC with a permanent establishment in Alberta must allocate income to Alberta using the Alberta allocation formulae in the Income Tax Act (Alberta). If the ULC has a PE in more than one province or country, compute the Alberta allocation factor based on gross revenue and salaries and wages attributable to Alberta. The Alberta return requires the filing of the T2SCH5 (corporation allocation among provinces and territories).

field_by_field_filling_dissection.line_or_box_code: T2SCH5 / T2SCH5S: Provincial and territorial allocation and exemption
field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Allocation of taxable income and taxable capital among provinces and territories, using the formulas of revenue and salaries/wages, with the special rules for a permanent establishment. Alberta requires the filing of the provincial allocation schedule to determine the portion of income taxed at the Alberta 8% rate.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: A ULC with operations outside Alberta must allocate income based on the permanent establishment rules, not based on the location of customers. DTC web sales do not for this purpose create a PE unless the corporation has employees, offices, or dependent agents in other provinces. If the ULC has a PE only in Alberta, allocate 100% of income to Alberta.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late filing penalty: 5% of the unpaid tax balance, plus 1% per full month up to 12 months. For repeat filers, the penalty may be increased to 10% plus 2% per full month. A separate penalty for failure to file an information return is CAD 25 per day, up to CAD 2,500 for a T2 return. Failure to file a T2 on time for a corporation can also trigger a penalty under subsection 162(1) of the ITA of CAD 250 or 5% of the tax payable, whichever is greater. If the corporation fails to file an information return such as Schedule 8 (shareholder information), the penalty is CAD 100 per day, up to CAD 2,000. If the corporation is a registered charity or has other registration obligations, additional penalties apply. Late payment interest: CRA prescribed rate (currently 9% for Q2 2025) compounded daily on balance due and instalments. Criminal wilful failure to file may result in fine of up to CAD 50,000 and/or imprisonment of up to 2 years. Alberta late filing penalty: 5% of Alberta tax payable, plus 1% per month up to 12 months, as imposed under the Alberta Tax Revenue Administration Act, SA 2014, c A-18.3, and the Alberta Income Tax Act, RSA 2000, c A-30. Alberta interest applies at the prescribed underpayment rate.

profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.statutory_dividend_wht_rate: Under subsection 212(2) of the ITA, a dividend paid by a Canadian-resident corporation to a non-resident shareholder is subject to Part XIII withholding tax at a statutory rate of 25% on the gross amount. For a ULC that is resident in Canada, this applies to distributions to non-resident shareholders, including deemed dividends on redemption or wind-up under subsection 84(2) and (3) of the ITA. Alberta does not impose a separate dividend withholding tax. For a non-resident ULC with a PE in Canada, a remittance of branch profits is treated as a dividend under subsection 219(1) of the ITA and is subject to the 25% Part XIII rate, reduced by treaty branch tax provisions to 5% under the Canada-US treaty if the non-resident owner is a US resident corporation and the business income is attributable to a PE.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.treaty_relief_application_protocol: To invoke reduced withholding tax under a Canada tax treaty (DTA), the payor must have the beneficial owner complete and sign a Canada Revenue Agency Form NR301 - Declaration of Eligibility for Benefits Under a Tax Treaty for a Non-Resident Taxpayer, or the applicable lower treaty rate form such as NR302 (for the US under the Canada-US tax treaty), NR303 (for a corporation or other entity), NR304, and the payer must obtain, keep, and provide the CRA with the certificate upon demand. The Form NR301/NR302/NR303 must be submitted to the CRA before the withholding rate reduction can be claimed. For automatic treaty relief, the payor applies the reduced rate if the non-resident provides the completed form with a valid foreign tax identification number. The CRA also requires that the foreign resident be the beneficial owner and that the resident meets the Limitation on Benefits provisions of the Convention between Canada and the United States of America with Respect to Taxes on Income and on Capital (Canada-US Treaty) or the relevant DTA. A certificate of residence (TRC) from the foreign tax authority must be provided when filing the NR301/NR302/NR303. The ULC payor must maintain the NR forms and the TRC in its books and records; failure to obtain a completed NR form can result in being assessed for the full 25% withholding, plus penalties and interest.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.cross_border_royalty_and_interest_wht: Royalties: Statutory Part XIII rate for royalties paid by a Canadian resident to a non-resident under subsection 212(1)(d) of the ITA is 25%. Treaty rate reduced to 10% under the Canada-US treaty for copyright royalties and patents, but 0% for certain computer software copyright royalties under Article 12 of the Canada-US treaty. Canada's domestic rate under new E-commerce rules may be 0% if the royalty is for the use of computer software, which is commonly the case for Shopify apps, theme licenses, and the use of trademark for brand marketing. Interest: Statutory withholding rate 25% under subsection 212(1)(b) of the ITA; treaty rate reduced to 15% under Article 11 of the Canada-US treaty, but 0% for arm's length interest, including portfolio interest, under Article XI of the old Canada-US treaty, if the interest is fully deductible and the recipient is the beneficial owner and the interest is not included in the income of a PE in Canada. For other treaty jurisdictions, rates vary between 10% and 15%. Management or administrative fees paid to a non-arm's length non-resident are subject to 25% withholding tax under subsection 212(1)(a) against a statutory rate of 25% and may be reduced to 15% under Article VII of the Canada-US Treaty or to nil under specific in-treaty language. Payments for services are generally not subject to Part XIII withholding if they are arm's length fees for services performed wholly outside Canada, but the services must be not connected to a Canadian permanent establishment.

transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.tp_documentation_threshold_local_currenc: Section 247 of the ITA and the Income Tax Regulations (Canada) require a ULC that enters into transactions with non-resident non-arm's length persons to prepare a contemporaneous Transfer Pricing Master File and Local File if the total value of the controlled transactions exceeds CAD 1,000,000 gross for the taxation year for a Canadian participant, or if the value of transactions with a single non-resident associated enterprise exceeds CAD 50,000 for those involving intangible property or management fees, CAD 100,000 for financial transactions, and CAD 250,000 for other goods and services. For an Alberta ULC using a Shopify DTC store, the relevant thresholds are: CICA-based TP documentation requirement arises if the total amount paid or payable to non-resident non-arm's length persons (including payments for Shopify app subscriptions, service fees, trademarks, software licenses, and purchasing agencies) exceeds CAD 1,000,000. For intercompany services, the threshold is CAD 50,000 for specified services. The CRA may also require a Master File if the multinational enterprise group (MNE) has annual consolidated gross revenue of at least CAD 500,000,000, and the Local File must be filed if the Canadian entity has controlled transactions exceeding the CAD 1,000,000 threshold. Although Alberta has no separate transfer pricing legislation, the CRA administers the Canadian transfer pricing penalties and documentation requirements under sections 247(3) and 247(4) of the ITA. The penalty is a reduction of the adjustment amount, commonly 10% of the gross denial, and is reduced by the amount of any documentation that is provided within a specified period. The penalty is imposed in addition to the tax, under subsection 247(3), and can be as high as 10% of the adjustment amount, plus interest.
approved_arm_length_methodologies: Income method (for intangible property, including the Canadian mark-to-market election under Treasury Regulations §1.482-7)
transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.economic_substance_doctrine: Canada does not have a general Economic Substance Regulations (ESR) regime like the United Arab Emirates, but the CRA has anti-avoidance rules and the general anti-avoidance rule (GAAR) under section 245 of the ITA that deny the tax benefit of transactions that would artificially reduce tax without real economic substance. Alberta does not have a separate economic substance doctrine. For a ULC, the CRA examines whether the entity is a 'shell company' or a conduit with no real commercial activity, which can trigger reassessment under GAAR, the 'sham' doctrine, and the 'agency' doctrine. A ULC must demonstrate an adequate level of substance through actual operations, business premises, employees, customer contact, bank accounts, and inventory or service capacity to sustain the tax filing position. The Economic Substance Doctrine in Canada is not an explicit legal statute; rather, the CRA applies the 'place of effective management' and 'business purpose' tests under common law and the OECD BEPS principals. The Canada Revenue Agency's administrative policy in IC 88-2, 'General Anti-Avoidance Rule', states that the GAAR may be applied when a transaction is an avoidance transaction, the avoidance transaction results directly or indirectly in a tax benefit, and the transaction is void or substantially void as regards to its real business purpose. If the ULC is viewed as a 'treaty shopping' entity, the Canada-US treaty Limitation on Benefits clause (Article 29) may deny treaty benefits and subject the ULC to 25% withholding. The Canada Revenue Agency also has the authority under subsection 247(2) to recompute the arm's length price where the terms and conditions of the transaction would not have been entered into by arm's length persons.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Tax Evasion (Wilful Non-Filing or False Return)
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Intentionally failing to file a T2 return, under-reporting Shopify revenues, inflating expenses, claiming personal expenses as business deductions, using undisclosed foreign bank accounts, or signing a false T2 return.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Wilful evasion is an indictable offence under section 239(1) of the ITA: fine of 50% to 200% of the tax evaded and/or imprisonment for up to 2 years. Civil penalties under subsection 163(2) increase to 50% of the understated tax if the conduct is grossly negligent. The CRA may also impose the 'penalty of the highest amount' under subsection 163(1) for repeated omissions. Alberta will impose a corresponding provincial penalty on the provincial portion of the tax. CRA's Criminal Investigations Program may freeze bank accounts and seize assets.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors may be personally liable for the corporation's assessed tax, interest, and penalties under subsections 227.1(1) and 160(1) of the ITA if they failed to deduct, withhold, remit, or pay source deductions and GST/HST. For a ULC, shareholders may also have unlimited liability; the corporate veil does not shield sole shareholders from the debts of the corporation under the Alberta Business Corporations Act. Directors who committed or acquiesced in the evasion may also be personally liable for the 50% penalty under subsection 163(2) and be subject to a travel ban under the Canada Evidence Act and the Mutual Legal Assistance in Criminal Matters Act, and to extradition. Imprisonment for up to 5 years is possible for tax evasion where fraud is proven.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Transfer Pricing Documentation Failure / Thin Capitalization
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Failing to maintain contemporaneous TP documentation, charging non-arm's length management fees to a non-resident parent without justification, or deducting interest from a non-resident shareholder where the debt-to-equity ratio exceeds 1.5:1 (under subsection 18(4) of the ITA for payments to specified non-residents, supplemented by the earnings-stripping rules of subsection 18.2(1) introduced by Bill C-59 for years after October 7, 2016).
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: TP adjustment under section 247(2) in the amount of the difference between the arm's length price and the price charged; the adjustment is added to income. Penalty under subsection 247(3) is 10% of the gross adjustment amount, without a reduction for any offsetting adjustment, if the taxpayer fails to make or provide accurate records. Denial of interest deduction under the thin capitalization rules (subsection 18(4)) and an additional recharacterization penalty of 50% under subsection 18.2(5) if the interest is disallowed and not properly reported. Failure to file the required information return may also result in penalties under section 162(7) and the CRA can require a contemporaneous valuation study.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who signed the TP documents and were aware of the false information may be liable as 'persons who made or signed the return' under subsection 247(3) for the penalty. The CRA can assess directors personally under subsection 160(1) only for the unpaid tax of the corporation, not for the TP penalty unless the director is a person who participated in the avoidance transaction. Shareholders of a ULC are personally liable for the corporation's unpaid tax debts if the corporation has been struck from the register or if the shareholders received a distribution while insolvent, under the Alberta ABCA fraud provisions.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Shell Company / Lack of Economic Substance / Sham
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Incorporating an Alberta ULC solely to hold Shopify assets, bank accounts, trademarks, or contracts for the benefit of a non-resident owner without any real office, employees, inventory, management, business decisions, or operational risk, and then using treaty or domestic law to avoid Canadian taxation; presenting a non-existent business office, or directing that transactions be recorded in a corporation's books with instructions to conceal the true principal.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Under the sham doctrine and GAAR (section 245 of the ITA), the CRA may disregard the ULC and attribute all income, gains, expenses, and credits to the person who really earned them, resulting in full taxation at the owner's personal rate plus interest and the 50% gross negligence penalty. The CRA may also apply the 'Canadian-controlled private corporation' rules and revoke treaty benefits under the Canada-US Treaty Limitation on Benefits provision. The corporate entity may be considered not to have a permanent establishment, and the non-resident may be assessed under section 2(3) as carrying on business in Canada, attracting retroactive Part I tax, Part XIII withholding, branch tax under section 219, and a 10% penalty under section 247(3) if pricing is adjusted. Striking a ULC off the Alberta register for failure to file annual returns (Alberta Corporate Registry) does not extinguish shareholder liability; the corporate veil is ignored when the 'piercing the corporate veil' doctrine applies in equity or for tax fraud.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: A director or controlling shareholder who knowingly operates a sham ULC may be jointly and severally liable under the ABCA for torts, fraud, and trust fund breaches. The CRA can impose personal liability under subsection 160(1) for any transfer of property from the corporation to a shareholder for less than fair market value while the corporation owed tax, which occurs if the ULC pays no dividends while transferring cash to a parent. The corporate veil is pierced for fraud, and directors of the ULC may be personally liable for unpaid GST/HST and payroll source deductions, including fines up to CAD 50,000 and imprisonment for 2 years under subsection 227.1(1). Travel bans and surrender of passports can be ordered in criminal tax proceedings.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Paying dividends to non-resident shareholders without withholding the statutory 25% Part XIII tax, or structuring distributions as loans, management fees, royalties, or service payments between the ULC and a non-resident parent without a Canadian withholding obligation; failing to file the required NR4 information returns; issuing a demand loan that exceeds a 90-day period, triggering deemed dividends under subsection 15(2) of the ITA.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: The non-resident payee is liable for Part XIII tax of 25% on the gross amount of the dividend or deemed dividend. The payer (the ULC) is liable for withholding the tax and remitting it by the 15th day of the month after the payment; failure to remit results in a penalty equal to 10% of the amount not remitted, plus interest, and a second penalty of 20% if the CRA sends a demand and the amount is not remitted within 90 days. The ULC is also liable for the gross amount of withheld tax, and the non-resident can be assessed under section 227(8) of the ITA. Failure to file NR4 summaries and information returns attracts a penalty of CAD 100 per day, capped at CAD 2,000, and penalties for false statements. Unpaid Part XIII tax can be assessed against the ULC directors personally under subsection 227.1(1).
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors and officers who knowingly participate in the non-withholding of Part XIII tax are personally liable for the full amount of the withholding, plus penalties and interest. In addition, the transfer of profits to a non-resident owner without withholding contravenes subsection 160(1); the non-resident transferee may be liable for the amount of the tax that the ULC failed to remit. If the ULC is used as a flow-through vehicle and the division of profits is a sham, the non-resident owner will be assessed personally under the ITA and the directors may be prosecuted. Alberta provincial penalty: late remittance of the Alberta provincial portion if any, and the CRA may issue a 'penalty for failure to remit' up to 20% of the unremitted amount. Imprisonment up to 2 years applies to each count of currency concealment under the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act if the transaction is designed to avoid the reporting threshold.
